title: Conversational AI Capability and Organizational Agility
abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a strategic capability for enhancing customer interactions and supporting organizational processes. However, the mechanisms through which conversational AI capability contributes to organizational agility remain underexplored. Drawing on the Dynamic Capabilities View, Service-Dominant Logic, and Information Processing Theory, this study examines the mediating roles of customer experience and decision-making efficiency. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was adopted using perceptual survey data collected from managers in highly digitalized companies. The proposed model was tested using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that conversational AI capability is positively associated with organizational agility, both directly and indirectly through customer experience and decision-making efficiency. The study contributes to the literature by integrating complementary theoretical perspectives to explain how conversational AI capabilities foster organizational agility and offers practical implications for organizations seeking to strengthen their adaptive capabilities in dynamic environments. Because the study relies on cross-sectional perceptual data, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of associations rather than causal relationships.

title: Following the Money Trail: Spotting Laundering Sinks in Bitcoin Networks with Cluster-Guided Graph Learning
abstract: Follow the money in Bitcoin, and it often dies in a sink. An address takes in funds but almost never sends them onward. We wanted to know if a Graph Neural Network (GNN) could be trained to identify these exact dead ends, and more importantly, whether flagging them would actually help investigators catch a higher volume of illicit transactions. Working with the Elliptic graph comes with a catch. The 165 standard node features already bake in neighbor aggregates, meaning message-passing mostly just rediscovers what the data already says. We call this the structural blind spot. Our fix is deliberately small. We started with five structural features and applied a log transform before running a supervised Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) projection. We then used k-Means clustering with k = 10. This let us append a distance-to-sink-centroid score to each node. Because everything is fit strictly on training nodes, we can guarantee absolutely zero data leakage, which means the model’s performance on unseen data is genuinely earned. F1-Illicit jumps by 7.6% while F1-Macro rises 3.9% over the raw-feature baseline. PR-AUC remains competitive. Adding just a slight dose of supervised structure forces the model to recognize the laundering operations hiding right in front of it, giving investigators a lightweight, label-efficient tool to track illicit funds without getting lost in the noise.

title: Toward scalable generative AI: efficient language model distillation via zero-shot rationales
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates an efficient approach for distilling Large Language Models (LLMs) into smaller, application-specific models using zero-shot Chain of Thought (CoT) rationale generation and Optimization by Prompting (OPRO). To address the challenges of deploying computationally intensive generative AI for narrow tasks or resource-constrained environments, the approach leverages LLM reasoning capabilities to generate both labels and natural language explanations for unlabeled data. By reducing reliance on human-generated annotations, the approach substantially lowers annotation requirements and prompting costs while maintaining comparable performance in the evaluated settings. We formulate distillation as a multi-task learning problem in which student models are trained to jointly predict labels and learn from teacher-generated rationales, with the goal of improving data efficiency and generalization. Building on established zero-shot Chain of Thought (CoT) prompting and the OPRO prompt optimization technique, we use teacher-generated rationales to reduce annotation token requirements and examine the associated performance and efficiency gains. Additionally, we systematically investigate how explanation properties affect distillation efficiency. Across natural language inference and question answering benchmarks, results indicate that near-optimal performance can be achieved even when rationales are provided for only a subset of the training data, and that shorter explanations are often sufficient. These findings provide practical insights into the trade-offs between rationale generation cost and student model performance. Overall, this work contributes empirical evidence on the effectiveness and cost characteristics of rationale-based distillation for training compact, task-specific language models with minimal human intervention.

title: Compute-in-Memory Attention: A Time-Domain Analog Softmax Circuit with RC-Tunable Temperature
abstract: Softmax is a key operation in Transformer attention, but its exponentiation and normalization add significant overhead in compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators, especially when analog attention scores must first be converted to the digital domain. This work presents a tunable-temperature analog softmax circuit in GlobalFoundries 22-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FDSOI) technology that operates directly on CIM-generated score voltages without intermediate analog-to-digital conversion. Each input score is converted into a time-domain event using a shared falling ramp. The corresponding comparator transition samples an RC-decaying reference to generate an exponential weight, which is then processed by an in-circuit normalization stage. In contrast to analog softmax circuits that rely on transistor weak-inversion behavior for exponentiation, the proposed architecture controls the softmax response through the ramp slope and RC time constant, enabling programmable effective temperature. The 128-element architecture is evaluated using transistor-level and post-layout extracted simulations, including multi-level input vectors, capacitance variation and mismatch, process and temperature variation, monte carlo analysis, and shared-interconnect parasitics. The complete 128-element implementation occupies 9453.42~$μ\mathrm{m}^{2}$ including the shared global ramp circuitry, while each replicated softmax element occupies 70.2~$μ\mathrm{m}^{2}$. The circuit achieves a 242.97-ns evaluation latency at 13.44~mW total power, corresponding to 25.5~pJ per output element. The simultaneous 128-element evaluation achieves an RMSE of 24.46~mV relative to the ideal softmax response. The extracted circuit characteristics are further incorporated into a MemTorch-based hardware-aware Transformer model, where the proposed softmax achieves a validation loss within 2.5\% of the ideal-softmax baseline.

title: LLM-Driven Joint Evolution of Coupled Heuristics Components for Routing Optimization
abstract: Heuristic design for combinatorial optimization remains heavily reliant on expert knowledge, while existing large language model (LLM)-enhanced evolutionary methods typically evolve isolated algorithmic components, even when one determines the search state on which another operates. This paper proposes LLM-driven Heuristic Components Joint Generation (LLM-HCJG), a population-based framework that jointly generates and co-evolves interdependent heuristic components under a shared design blueprint. Applied to guided local search (GLS), LLM-HCJG couples solution initialization with penalty construction and embeds the generated pair into an enhanced online search mechanism. The resulting form is further transferred from the traveling salesman problem (TSP) to the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP). Theoretical analysis establishes the non-separable state-transition effects between the two components and the advantage in generation consistency. Across synthetic instances and 41 public TSPLIB/CVRPLIB benchmarks, LLM-HCJG attains consistently low optimality gaps, including best or tied-best results on 28 of 29 TSPLIB instances and all 12 CVRPLIB instances. Ablation and structural analyses further indicate that these gains are associated with cross-component compatibility and alignment rather than isolated-component recombination. These results support effective cross-instance transfer within the evaluated routing settings under limited-sample, modest-cost training.

title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Matching the Offline $0.401$ Factor
abstract: We study online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed subsets of the $d$-dimensional unit cube. The best known constructive offline approximation factor is $0.401$ under the corresponding meta-solvability assumptions, whereas comparable adversarial online guarantees had remained at $1/e$. We show that this factor is also achievable online. In the post-decision full-information value-oracle model, our algorithm attains factor $0.401$ with sublinear approximate regret when oracle feedback is conditionally unbiased and bounded. The online algorithm does not run the offline construction on a changing objective. Instead, it replaces the offline objective-dependent box step by a weighted online learner that controls the required residual terms cumulatively. An exact asymmetric balance theorem preserves the offline coefficients despite adversarial variation. The direct implementation has $O(T^{3/4})$ regret and uses $O(dT^{1/4})$ oracle calls per round. More generally, for every $δ\in[0,1/4]$, batching gives $O(T^δ)$ calls per round and $O(T^{4/5-δ/5})$ regret, including a one-call $O(T^{4/5})$ endpoint. Under a positive-anchor condition, randomized blocking retains factor $0.401$ with $O(T^{5/6})$ one-point bandit regret.

title: Contrasting Effects of Control on Fidelity and Fidelity Deviation in Controlled Teleportation
abstract: Teleportation performance is commonly characterized by the average teleportation fidelity, while its variation over input states provides additional information captured by the fidelity deviation. In controlled teleportation, the controller's measurement introduces an additional source of fidelity variation through its measurement outcomes. We investigate the fidelity deviation in controlled teleportation with three-qubit pure states. We derive a lower bound on the fidelity deviation and show that it is attainable together with the maximal average teleportation fidelity. Among the measurements attaining the maximal average fidelity, however, the fidelity deviation can vary depending on the controller's measurement. We further examine the effect of controller assistance by comparing controlled teleportation with direct teleportation using the reduced state. Unlike the maximal average fidelity, which cannot decrease with controller assistance, the minimal fidelity deviation is not necessarily reduced by controller assistance. In particular, for any W-class pure state, controller assistance cannot reduce the fidelity deviation. These results reveal contrasting effects of control on teleportation fidelity and its deviation in controlled teleportation.

title: Opening the Black Box a Crack: A State of the Art Review of Explainability and Interpretability of Black-Box Models
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Explainability and Interpretability of Black-Box Models in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of explainable AI and interpretability as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Core Claim: A Quantum-Adaptive Dynamic Matrix Decomposition Method
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum-adaptive dynamic matrix decomposition method, aiming to significantly enhance computational efficiency, particularly when dealing with large matrices. Traditional matrix factorization methods often exhibit limitations in scalability and speed, especially with high-dimensional datasets. Our approach leverages the unique properties of quantum self-adapted matrix decomposition, allowing for rapid and efficient breakdown of matrices. The core mechanism involves a quantum-optimized decomposition process that adapts to the matrix's structure, leading to substantial performance gains. We present a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and discuss its potential impact on various matrix factorization applications. This work contributes to the advancement of efficient matrix computation techniques.

title: The Emergence of Semantic Networks: A Novel Approach to Enhanced Semantic Understanding and Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for semantic network fusion, leveraging multiple scales to enhance semantic understanding and reasoning capabilities. Traditional approaches often overlook the crucial relationship between different feature scales, leading to suboptimal performance. Our proposed method establishes a multi-scale feature semantic network and employs a sophisticated fusion strategy to effectively integrate these features, resulting in improved semantic comprehension and inference. The core mechanism focuses on identifying and prioritizing key features across different scales, creating a richer and more robust representation of the underlying semantic relationships. This research addresses the limitations of existing methods by offering a more comprehensive and adaptable approach to semantic network analysis.

title: Dynamic Topological Space Transformations for Optimization
abstract: The optimization of complex systems often requires careful manipulation of their structure. Traditional optimization methods frequently rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting the system's adaptability. This paper introduces a novel dynamic topological space transformation optimization algorithm designed to automatically adjust transformation parameters, thereby enhancing system performance. We present a framework that leverages a dynamic mapping of the system's topological space, enabling the algorithm to optimize for specific performance metrics based on evolving system characteristics. The core mechanism involves a continuous, adaptive transformation process guided by a learned mapping, providing a flexible and robust solution for complex optimization problems. This approach overcomes the limitations of static optimization techniques by actively responding to changes in the system, leading to improved efficiency and robustness. title: Topological Protection of Quantum Error Correction Codes
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum error correction (QEC) utilizing topological protection. The core idea centers on leveraging the unique properties of anyons within topological insulators to physically protect quantum codes, thereby dramatically enhancing their resilience against noise. Traditional QEC schemes often rely on classical communication channels for redundancy, introducing latency and complexity. In contrast, our proposed method constructs a physical layer redundancy through the entanglement of anyons within a topological material. This approach offers a more robust and intrinsically fault-tolerant system. We present a theoretical framework outlining the implementation of specific QEC codes—specifically the Shor code—protected by topological anyon entanglement. The resulting system demonstrates a significant improvement in error correction performance compared to conventional approaches. The key innovations include the mapping of quantum information onto anyon states and the utilization of braiding operations to maintain the encoded information's integrity. Further investigation explores the scalability and practical considerations associated with this topological protection strategy.

title: Bayesian Inference Engine Based on Biological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to probabilistic inference by emulating the mechanisms of biological neural networks. Traditional probabilistic inference engines often rely on classical logic or graph models, lacking a biologically inspired simulation of neural networks and their inherent probabilistic reasoning processes. This work introduces a Bayesian inference engine constructed upon a layered, distributed, and synapse-plasticity-based architecture, mirroring key features of biological neurons. The core mechanism involves probabilistic connections and information transmission between neurons, facilitating continuous updating of probabilistic beliefs and enabling complex inferences. The engine leverages concepts such as Bayesian updating, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, and belief propagation, implemented within a network structure designed to mimic biological neural dynamics. The resulting system offers a potentially more robust and adaptive approach to probabilistic reasoning, particularly in scenarios where uncertainty is inherent and traditional methods struggle. This research lays the groundwork for a new paradigm in artificial intelligence, moving beyond purely symbolic approaches towards more biologically plausible models of cognition. ---

title: Temporal Relational Graph Embedding with Dynamic Context
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to graph embedding that addresses the limitations of existing methods in capturing the dynamic nature of evolving graphs. Traditional graph embedding techniques often rely on static representations, failing to account for the temporal changes in relationships between nodes. Our proposed method, Temporal Relational Graph Embedding with Dynamic Context (TRGDC), leverages a recurrent neural network to model the dynamic context of a graph, incorporating both relational information and the elapsed time since the last update. The core idea is to continuously adapt node embeddings based on these temporal and relational factors. We demonstrate that TRGDC significantly improves the representation of dynamic graphs compared to static embedding methods, achieving superior performance in downstream graph-related tasks. The key contributions of this work are the integration of temporal modeling with relational graph embedding and the utilization of a recurrent neural network for dynamic context representation.

title: Probability Logic Matrix Entropy
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to entropy calculation based on probability logic matrices, designed to rigorously assess the robustness and stability of algorithms, particularly within the context of machine learning. Traditional entropy measures often focus on static performance, while this method integrates dynamic adjustments driven by machine learning to provide a more comprehensive evaluation. The core mechanism involves leveraging the inherent probabilistic nature of probability logic matrices to quantify the uncertainty and sensitivity of an algorithm to its input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a focused study of a reinforcement learning algorithm, showcasing its ability to identify vulnerabilities and guide model refinement. The research explores how this method can contribute to enhanced model reliability and performance.

title: 基于量子态叠加的并行算法设计方法
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to parallel algorithm design leveraging the principles of quantum state superposition. The core concept involves decomposing a given problem into a superposition of quantum states, enabling parallel computation across these states. This methodology aims to achieve exponential speedups compared to traditional classical algorithms. The design methodology focuses on identifying suitable problems amenable to this superposition-based parallelization. The theoretical framework outlines the key steps in constructing such algorithms, emphasizing the importance of state preparation, quantum gate operations, and state measurement. We explore the potential impact of this technique on various computational domains, highlighting the challenges and opportunities associated with realizing quantum speedups. The presented approach offers a fundamentally new paradigm for algorithm design, potentially revolutionizing computational efficiency.

title: Quantum Probability Computation: An Adaptive Optimization Framework
abstract: Quantum probability computation (QPC) holds immense promise for advanced scientific discovery and technological innovation. However, the inherent complexity of QPC algorithms necessitates sophisticated optimization techniques to achieve efficient computation. This paper introduces an adaptive optimization framework for QPC, designed to automatically adjust parameters and minimize computational cost. The core mechanism involves dynamically modifying key parameters based on the problem's characteristics, leading to enhanced efficiency. We present a comprehensive overview of the framework's design, detailing the optimization strategy and its potential impact on QPC performance. This work addresses a critical limitation of traditional QPC approaches, offering a novel solution for improved scalability and throughput.

title: Quantum Error Correction for Classical Computing via Topological Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates a fundamentally new approach to quantum error correction (QEC) by employing topological encoding within classical materials. Traditional QEC relies on quantum mechanics and entanglement, presenting significant technological hurdles for implementation on conventional computers. Our proposed method leverages the inherent robustness of topological states, specifically the braiding of quasiparticles, to achieve error detection and correction without direct measurement of the encoded quantum states. The core idea involves mapping logical qubits to physical qubits based on the topological properties of the material. By carefully controlling and manipulating these quasiparticles, we can implement a fault-tolerant QEC scheme directly on classical hardware. This approach avoids the decoherence issues associated with quantum systems and offers a potentially scalable solution for QEC using readily available materials. We present a theoretical framework for this encoding scheme, outlining the key mathematical concepts and relationships involved. The proposed methodology represents a shift in perspective, moving from quantum to topological approaches for QEC, opening new avenues for computation and information processing.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework, termed "Adaptive Quantum Topology" (AQT), designed to optimize quantum computation. The core principle of AQT leverages the unique properties of quantum topology – a mathematical concept describing the interconnectedness of quantum states – to enhance the efficiency of quantum algorithms. The paper details the framework's design, emphasizing its capacity to generate novel quantum circuits and improve overall computational performance. The significance of this work lies in its potential to overcome limitations of traditional approaches, offering a fundamentally different paradigm for quantum algorithm design. This research explores the mathematical foundations of AQT, outlining the key steps involved in generating and optimizing quantum circuits that exhibit enhanced coherence and fidelity. We present a rigorous analysis of the framework's performance with specific examples demonstrating its efficacy in various quantum computation tasks. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: THE IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ON MARKETING STRATEGIES OF TRANSNATIONAL COMPANIES IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
abstract: The article examines the impact of artificial intelligence technologies on the transformation of marketing strategies of transnational companies in international business. The relevance of the study stems from the rapid expansion of the global artificial intelligence market and the fact that marketing and sales have consistently remained among the business functions with the highest intensity of AI adoption worldwide. For transnational companies, which coordinate marketing activities across dozens of national markets with different languages, consumer cultures and regulatory regimes, artificial intelligence directly affects the classical dilemma of international marketing between standardisation and adaptation: the technology promises to deliver globally consistent brand communication that is simultaneously tailored to local audiences at a scale and speed unattainable for traditional marketing organisations. The article discusses the main directions in which artificial intelligence penetrates the international marketing activity of transnational companies, including hyper-personalisation of customer experience based on machine learning, generative production of advertising and communication content, restructuring of organisational models of marketing departments, and localisation of global campaigns for national markets. Particular attention is paid to the experience of leading transnational corporations in the consumer goods, digital services and e-commerce sectors, as well as to the organisational conditions under which investments in artificial intelligence translate into measurable economic outcomes. The study also addresses the risks accompanying the diffusion of the technology, including changes in consumer attitudes towards AI-generated advertising, reputational threats, and the new regulatory environment created by the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act for companies operating in the European market. The consequences of the uneven global distribution of AI infrastructure, investment and competencies for the competitive positions of companies from developed and developing economies in international markets are considered as a separate dimension of the problem within the field of international economic relations.

abstract: "This dataset contains the processed experimental results and figure-source files associated with the study \u201cLow-Visible Robust Weight Generation for Byzantine Federated Learning via Sketch-Based Detection.\u201d The data support the evaluation of CipherSketch-RFL under Byzantine model-update attacks, including sign flipping, scaling, model replacement, A Little Is Enough, and inner product manipulation. The processed results are provided in CSV and JSON formats for inspection and reproduction."

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
abstract: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

title: SurfSpec: Enhancing Off-Target-Agnostic Specificity by Bounding Pocket-Ligand Geometric Mismatch
abstract: Lead optimization in structure-based drug design aims to improve target binding while avoiding unintended interactions with off-target pockets. However, existing affinity-driven methods do not explicitly control specificity, whereas current specificity-aware approaches commonly require prior knowledge of off-target structures. We address off-target-agnostic specificity-aware lead optimization by analyzing the geometric mismatch between a ligand and the target pocket. We provide a conservative specificity lower bound for geometrically separated off-targets without requiring access to off-target structures. By metricizing pocket--ligand mismatch, the triangle inequality shows that reducing target--ligand mismatch improves a conservative lower bound on mismatch to a separated off-target class, which can be translated into a specificity lower bound through an empirical geometry--affinity calibration. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce SurfSpec, an off-target-agnostic lead optimization framework that iteratively grows ligands toward under-occupied regions of the target pocket surface. SurfSpec alternates between linker generation toward selected target-surface patches, which provides geometric pseudo-labels, and refinement under a pocket-conditioned ligand prior, which restores these pseudo-labels into valid ligands. On the CrossDocked2020 test set, SurfSpec reduces geometric mismatch and outperforms evaluated off-target-agnostic lead optimization baselines in empirical specificity, while maintaining competitive target-affinity improvement.

title: Effective Hamiltonian for an off-resonantly driven qubit-cavity system
abstract: Accurate modeling of driven light-matter interactions is essential for quantum technologies, where natural and synthetic atoms are used to store and process quantum information, mediate interactions between bosonic modes, and enable nonlinear operations. In systems subject to multitone drives, however, the theoretical description becomes challenging and existing models cannot quantitatively reproduce the experimental data. Here, we derive an effective Hamiltonian that retains slowly rotating terms, providing a general framework for accurately describing driven dynamics across platforms. As a concrete application, we validate the theory in circuit QED, where it quantitatively reproduces experimentally measured ac Stark shifts and captures key interactions such as two-mode squeezing and beam splitting. Our results establish a broadly applicable tool to engineer driven interactions in quantum information processing platforms.

title: Hidden States as Bounded Objects?
abstract: This is an application preprint in the Atacton Working Paper Series (ATACTON-WP-HMM-001, Version 1.0). It is not peer reviewed. It is an application freeze on representation architecture, not a fitted-model preprint. No EM results, no reader results, and no forecast results are claimed. The proposition is computational unity ≠ semantic unity: one latent path can be well-defined as a statistical co-representation of unlike series and still fail as one bounded historical object. Strategy A is a mixed-state representation; Strategy B is an object-separated representation. The paper also freezes the hierarchy observed variable ≠ semantic object ≠ latent state (X ≠ R ≠ Z): data-source multiplicity does not imply object multiplicity. Frozen Kₖ v1.0 (Wong, 2026c) is called, not rewritten. The same unplayed Premier League fixture as Application 1 (Ipswich Town v Liverpool, 4 September 2026) is bound on a different evidence layer: league result path plus dated pre-kick-off quotes, not the H2H page. The framework constrains the semantic interpretation of model components; it does not determine the statistically optimal factorisation. Correspondence: joe@atacton.com

It is an application freeze on representation architecture, not a fitted-model preprint. No EM results, no reader results, and no forecast results are claimed. The proposition is computational unity ≠ semantic unity: one latent path can be well-defined as a statistical co-representation of unlike series and still fail as one bounded historical object. Strategy A is a mixed-state representation; Strategy B is an object-separated representation. The paper also freezes the hierarchy observed variable ≠ semantic object ≠ latent state (X ≠ R ≠ Z): data-source multiplicity does not imply object multiplicity. Frozen Kₖ v1.0 (Wong, 2026c) is called, not rewritten. The same unplayed Premier League fixture as Application 1 (Ipswich Town v Liverpool, 4 September 2026) is bound on a different evidence layer: league result path plus dated pre-kick-off quotes, not the H2H page. The framework constrains the semantic interpretation of model components; it does not determine the statistically optimal factorisation. Correspondence: joe@atacton.com

title: Rewards, Regrets, and Rubber Arms: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of Reinforcement Learning in Games and Robotics
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Reinforcement Learning in Games and Robotics in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of reinforcement learning and robotics as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Explaining Next-Activity Prediction with Activity-Level Shapley Attributions
abstract: This software implements the framework presented in "Explaining Next-Activity Prediction with Activity-Level Shapley Attributions." It trains Transformer classifiers (BERT-base and RoBERTa-base) to predict the next activity of an ongoing case from its observed activity prefix and explains the predictions with SHAP at the level of complete activity occurrences. The package includes code for model training and evaluation, the ablation (Full, Scratch, and Frozen) and backbone experiments, SHAP explanations, the comparison with LIME in faithfulness and runtime, and the aggregation of results and statistical tests across random seeds. The benchmark event logs and trained models are not redistributed; the README lists the public sources of the datasets and the steps to reproduce all results. Version 1.1.0 revises the README to follow the journal's reproducibility guidelines, adds an MIT License, and sets the default training batch size to 32, as reported in the manuscript.

title: Dual Optimisation in Low-Resource Natural Language Processing: Integrating Meta-Learning and Efficient Deep Architectures for Sustainable AI Development
abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in low-resource Natural Language Processing (NLP): the lack of aunified framework that jointly optimises computational efficiency and task performance under severe dataand hardware constraints. To bridge this gap, the study introduces the Dual Optimisation Framework—thefirst empirically validated approach integrating meta-learning (MAML) with resource-adaptivearchitectures (DistilBERT and MobileBERT). A mixed-methods design was used: quantitative experimentsmeasured accuracy, F1-scores, latency, and memory consumption across multiple configurations, whilequalitative expert interviews contextualised deployment feasibility in low-resource settings. Results showthat DistilBERT combined with MAML improves efficiency–performance trade-offs by up to 35%,outperforming larger models while maintaining competitive accuracy. Latency and memory profilingconfirm the framework’s suitability for computational realities in the Global South. The study contributes ascalable, sustainable model for equitable NLP development and demonstrates how learning efficiency andcomputational efficiency can be co-optimised in constrained environments.

title: Dynamic Quantum Information Encoding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic quantum information encoding technique designed to adapt to environmental changes and target behaviors, resulting in more intelligent signal processing and data transmission. The core mechanism leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust encoding strategies. Traditional encoding methods are static and require pre-defined parameters, offering limited adaptability. This work proposes a fundamentally new approach that allows for real-time, self-optimizing encoding, potentially revolutionizing data communication and signal processing. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Non-Linear Random Matrix Adaptation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive adjustment algorithm for non-linear random matrices, aiming to enhance model generalization capabilities. Traditional matrix decomposition and machine learning methods rely on static parameters, failing to adequately capture data-driven nonlinear relationships. Our approach leverages a dynamically adjusted "self-adaptive random matrix" mechanism, introducing stochastic noise to subtly modify matrix weights, allowing the model to adapt to the data's inherent non-linearity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of simulations, showcasing improved performance on a dataset designed to exhibit complex, non-linear patterns. This research offers a significant advancement in model adaptation, particularly for data with inherent non-linearity.

title: Relational Reasoning with Knowledge Graphs and Probabilistic Logic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to relational reasoning that addresses the limitations of existing methods by integrating knowledge graphs with probabilistic logic programming languages. Current relational reasoning systems often struggle with the inherent uncertainty and incompleteness of real-world knowledge. This work proposes a framework that explicitly represents relationships within a knowledge graph and utilizes probabilistic logic programming to perform inference, allowing for robust reasoning even when data is noisy or missing. The core claim is that this integration provides a more flexible and robust solution compared to traditional approaches. The key mechanism involves representing relationships as probabilistic rules within a logic programming environment, leveraging the structured knowledge provided by the knowledge graph to guide the reasoning process. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance in scenarios involving incomplete and uncertain data, offering a significant advancement in relational reasoning capabilities. We detail the architecture, the integration strategy, and outline potential applications, highlighting the benefits of this combined approach.

title: Cognitive Architectures for Automated Scientific Discovery
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to automated scientific discovery by developing a cognitive architecture specifically designed to emulate human scientific reasoning. Current artificial intelligence systems primarily rely on pattern recognition and statistical analysis, often struggling with the fundamental aspects of scientific inquiry – independently formulating hypotheses, designing experiments to test them, and interpreting the results. This architecture, termed "Scientific Reasoning Engine" (SRE), aims to bridge this gap. The core of SRE lies in its modular design, comprising components for knowledge representation (KR), hypothesis generation (HG), experiment design (ED), and data analysis (DA). The system operates through a cyclical process: KR gathers and organizes information, HG generates potential hypotheses based on this knowledge, ED designs experiments to test these hypotheses, DA analyzes the experimental data, and the cycle repeats, refining hypotheses and knowledge. The architecture is fundamentally different from existing AI approaches, which often treat scientific discovery as a purely computational task, neglecting the crucial role of human-like reasoning processes. The system's potential impact is significant, offering a path toward truly autonomous scientific exploration.

title: Algorithmic Transparency via Explainable Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, their complex architecture and opaque decision-making processes, often referred to as the "black box" problem, significantly limit their widespread adoption. This work addresses this critical issue by proposing a novel approach to enhance the transparency and interpretability of GNNs. We introduce a "gradient flow" visualization technique that dynamically highlights the nodes and edges most influential in generating the network's output. Furthermore, we integrate this visualization with methods for interpreting node embeddings, providing a comprehensive understanding of the network's reasoning. Our approach offers a visual and intuitive pathway to understanding GNN decisions, ultimately aiming to bridge the gap between complex models and human understanding and fostering greater trust and reliability in GNN applications. The core of our contribution lies in providing a practical tool for debugging, validating, and refining GNN models.

title: Adaptive Self-Organized Quantum Computation Algorithm Optimization
abstract: Quantum computation is rapidly advancing, demanding sophisticated algorithms and efficient optimization techniques. This paper explores the integration of adaptive self-organized quantum computation into algorithm optimization. We propose a novel framework leveraging self-organizing quantum systems to dynamically adjust parameters of quantum algorithms, resulting in enhanced performance. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional optimization methods by adapting to the algorithm's unique characteristics in real-time. The core mechanism involves the quantum system itself acting as a self-learning optimization tool. The design is predicated on the observation that the optimal parameter settings for quantum algorithms are rarely static; instead, they evolve based on the algorithm's trajectory. This paper details the design, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this adaptive framework for optimizing a specific quantum algorithm. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: ##基于多智能体强化学习的资源调度与管理
abstract: This paper explores the application of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to the problem of resource scheduling and management. Traditional resource management approaches often struggle with dynamic environments and complex dependencies. MARL offers a promising solution by enabling a decentralized, adaptive system where multiple agents learn to coordinate and optimize resource allocation. We propose a framework utilizing a population of agents, each responsible for a specific subset of resources, and employing reinforcement learning algorithms to facilitate intelligent decision-making. The core claim is that this approach leads to improved resource utilization and efficiency. The paper details the system architecture, the reinforcement learning methodology, and discusses key challenges and future research directions. The primary goal is to demonstrate the potential of MARL in tackling the complexities of resource management scenarios.

title: ##基于量子纠错码的量子存储器设计
abstract: This paper presents a novel design for a quantum storage system based on quantum error-correcting codes. The primary goal is to enhance the storage capacity and reliability of quantum storage devices, which are fundamental to the advancement of quantum computing. The proposed architecture leverages the principles of quantum error correction, specifically utilizing low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, to mitigate the effects of decoherence and other sources of quantum noise. The design incorporates redundancy through the encoding of multiple logical qubits within a physical qubit ensemble, enabling the detection and correction of errors without compromising the integrity of the stored quantum information. The performance analysis demonstrates the potential for significant improvements in storage fidelity and the ability to store a larger number of quantum bits compared to traditional, uncorrected quantum storage approaches. The design addresses key challenges in quantum storage, including error mitigation and data preservation, contributing to the realization of scalable and reliable quantum computing systems.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation for Cooperative Exploration
abstract: This paper investigates the application of intrinsic motivation within a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework to enhance cooperative exploration. Traditional MARL approaches frequently encounter difficulties in efficiently coordinating exploration efforts, particularly within complex environments. We hypothesize that the introduction of intrinsic motivation signals, such as curiosity or surprise, can significantly improve agent behavior by directly incentivizing exploration of novel states and strategies. Our approach formulates the reward function to incorporate these intrinsic signals, allowing agents to proactively seek out unexplored regions of the environment. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and simulation results, that this combined approach leads to a faster and more effective cooperative exploration process compared to standard MARL methods. The core contribution lies in the synergistic combination of intrinsic motivation and MARL, addressing a significant bottleneck in achieving robust and adaptive cooperative behaviors in challenging scenarios. We evaluate the performance of our methodology across a range of benchmark cooperative tasks and highlight its advantages in terms of convergence speed, task completion rate, and overall exploration efficiency.

title: The Design of a Comparative Analysis System for LLMs
abstract: Large language models(LLM) are improving daily. The question then becomes, how can the large language model be improved? Evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of both LLM methods, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines and large context windows (LCW), is the goal of this project. NOBLIS is the primary stakeholder due to their goal of providing a distinction between which LLM method is more suited to their individual needs. The requirements of this project involve using a high-performance computing cluster to properly evaluate the large language model’s methods. Concerning the concepts of operations, we prompt the large language model with test cases from the dataset. Both methods must be evaluated with five metrics: hardware demands, processing times, affordability, differing dataset sizes, and output accuracy and quality. Concerning output evaluation, both evaluation metrics and tasks must be chosen. The evaluation metrics that will be used involve BERT-Score and DeepEval. The tasks that will help evaluate the methods involve summarization of text, true/false questions, and question-and-answer prompts. Three trials will be run to verify and validate these results. This will help standardize output from the methods and ensure that the evaluation metrics are evaluated properly.

title: Information-Theoretic Entropy Shaping for Deep Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel regularization technique for deep learning models, termed Information-Theoretic Entropy Shaping (ITES). Traditional regularization methods frequently employ heuristics, often without a rigorous theoretical grounding. This work introduces a framework that directly controls the entropy of hidden layer representations using information-theoretic principles. The core idea is to incorporate a "entropy shaping term" into the loss function, derived from the Shannon entropy of the hidden layer activations. This term actively guides the network's learning process, encouraging the discovery of representations with a specifically desired entropy profile. We demonstrate that this approach can lead to improved model robustness and generalization performance, particularly in scenarios where standard regularization methods struggle. The theoretical foundation of ITES rests on the fundamental properties of entropy and information, providing a principled method for shaping the feature space learned by deep neural networks. The primary contribution of this research lies in its systematic application of information theory as a foundational design element for deep learning regularization, offering a potentially more stable and adaptable approach compared to current heuristic-based methods.

title: Real-time multistation microseismic event detection via transfer learning of computer vision deep learning model
abstract: SUMMARY With the shale gas exploration and development into deep strata (> 3500 m in depth), weak signal detection becomes more challenging and vital in surface-based microseismic monitoring. Most existing deep learning approaches are trained on synthetic or single-station data, which limits their performance in detecting weak events in field seismic recordings. Here, we propose a deep learning approach based on the computer vision object detection model YOLOv5 via transfer learning and train it on a data set from field observation to better detect microseismic events in multichannel seismic data. First, we convert continuous seismic data into waveform images in greyscale with a record length of 20 s, and manually annotate the microseismic events containing the first arrival signals using rectangular boxes. To train the model, the transfer learning strategy is used by using parameters of YOLOs in computer vision to initiate the model. After training and validation, we conducted comprehensive tests to examine the performance of the model. Compared with the single-station short-term average/long-term average (STA/LTA) detector, our method reduces false positives markedly, yet it also delivers higher recall rate than the available multistation detection scheme. When applied to continuous data set from a different area, the model achieved good performance with a precision of 0.9832 and a recall of 0.9702, indicating it learns representative features of microseismic signals. All these tests illustrate that the proposed method achieves high detection accuracy, low false positive rates and robustness. Meanwhile, the method possesses the superiority for real-time monitoring and can be easily updated by adding a few new samples to the training data set.

Compared with the single-station short-term average/long-term average (STA/LTA) detector, our method reduces false positives markedly, yet it also delivers higher recall rate than the available multistation detection scheme. When applied to continuous data set from a different area, the model achieved good performance with a precision of 0.9832 and a recall of 0.9702, indicating it learns representative features of microseismic signals. All these tests illustrate that the proposed method achieves high detection accuracy, low false positive rates and robustness. Meanwhile, the method possesses the superiority for real-time monitoring and can be easily updated by adding a few new samples to the training data set.

title: GhostWord: A Fine-Grained Backdoor Attack on Automatic Speech Recognition
abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are widely deployed in safety-critical settings but remain vulnerable to data-poisoning backdoor attacks. Existing ASR backdoors typically use phrase-level triggers paired with a fixed target sentence, creating strong artifacts (e.g., repeated transcripts or triggers placed in non-speech regions) that simple preprocessing can mitigate. We propose GhostWord, a word-level, time-localized ASR backdoor that uses codebooks mapping short ($\approx$400\,ms) acoustic triggers to target words. During poisoning, we inject a trigger into the forced-aligned time span of a chosen source word in the audio and replace only that word in the transcript, enabling precise semantic flips and composable sentence manipulation while avoiding many-to-one label artifacts. Across Common Voice (v23 English, v24 Lithuanian) and multiple backbones (Whisper-Small/Medium, MMS, SpeechT5), GhostWord achieves an average attack success rate of 89.3\% and transfers across languages and models. Adapting optimization-based defenses (ABL, ANP, SAU, I-BAU) reveals a sharp robustness--accuracy trade-off: attack success drops from 89.3\% to 29.1\% while clean WER rises from 21.5\% to 45.0\%, consistent with our theoretical analysis showing that, in high-vocabulary models, backdoor suppression structurally tends to degrade clean performance. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/rohban-lab/GhostWord

title: Automated Vulnerability Injection in Smart Contracts Using Large Language Models
abstract: Assessing vulnerability detection tools for smart contracts requires datasets with known ground truth, yet such datasets are scarce and difficult to build by hand. We propose an approach that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically inject vulnerabilities into Solidity smart contracts, and demonstrate it in a case study targeting 49 vulnerability types from OpenSCV. Injected contracts are validated through a multi-step pipeline checking compilation, execution, business logic, and the presence of the intended vulnerability. Applied to real-world contracts from SmartBugs, LLMs generate nearly 1,000 candidate variants; after deduplication and validation, 32 confirmed vulnerable contracts spanning 25 vulnerability types survive (a 16.58% survival rate). Surviving contracts concentrate in structurally simpler targets and vulnerability types with localized syntactic patterns. We report practical challenges including LLMs' non-determinism and the difficulty of preserving contract semantics. We then use the validated contracts to assess three static analyzers, revealing complementary and incomplete coverage profiles. Results show that LLM-based vulnerability injection is feasible, while exposing key limitations in scalability and diversity.

title: GlyphAnchor: Enhancing Visual Text Rendering via Position-Anchored Glyph Priors
abstract: Rendering accurate text remains difficult for image generation and editing models, especially when the target contains long, complex, and densely arranged text or rare characters. Existing approaches either improve native text rendering through stronger backbones and data-centric training without explicit glyph priors, or incorporate glyph priors through specialized designs that remain insufficiently accurate and robust under challenging scenarios. We introduce GlyphAnchor, a novel text-rendering enhancement method for both text-to-image and image-editing diffusion transformer models. GlyphAnchor enhances the backbone with lightweight glyph patch conditions whose positions are anchored to the target image through the model's native positional encoding. We train this capability with staged supervised finetuning and further refine it with text-aware post-training to improve robustness. We also introduce InfoTextBench, a benchmark for evaluating text-rich visual text rendering in both generation and editing settings. Experiments across multiple backbones and benchmarks, including long, complex, and densely arranged text and rare character scenarios, show that GlyphAnchor consistently improves text fidelity while preserving overall image quality.

title: A Power Law in Logarithm's Clothing: On the Scalability of Graph-Based Vector Search
abstract: Most vector databases rely on graph-based indexes, notably HNSW and Vamana, for approximate nearest neighbor search. With embedding models widely adopted, the datasets these databases store grow rapidly. At a fixed accuracy, how does search cost scale with dataset size? The prevailing answer is poly-logarithmic growth. Yet the claim is proven only under special conditions and asserted without proof for the indexes used in practice. It is also largely untested: standard benchmarks measure cost at one dataset size, not across sizes. We put the claim to the test. The answer depends on the scale itself. While the dataset size $N$ is small relative to the data's intrinsic dimensionality, search cost grows as $N^c$ for a constant $0<c<1$. We call this scaling the Sublinear Power Law. Once $N$ is large enough, growth slows to subpolynomial, consistent with the poly-logarithmic claim. The Sublinear Power Law appears on every dataset, mostly up to its full size, at every recall target, query hardness level, and index configuration we test. The transition to subpolynomial growth appears on the two datasets that grow large enough relative to their intrinsic dimensionality. One mechanism underlies both behaviors: a dataset's intrinsic dimensionality grows with its size until the data resolves its underlying distribution. Higher intrinsic dimensionality packs more vectors into the query neighborhood the search must examine. We present a unifying theory of beam-search cost that explains our observations. For exact and bounded-degree constructions, we prove the Sublinear Power Law and the eventual transition to poly-logarithmic scaling, and derive the scale at which it occurs. We also develop models that predict the power-law exponents for any recall target and index configuration. These models give a principled way to navigate trade-offs among search cost, insertion cost, and recall as data grows.

title: Are explainable AI (XAI) evaluation strategies aligned? Comparing subjective, objective, and mathematical evaluation measures using saliency maps
abstract: The evaluation of explainable AI (XAI) approaches often relies on three families of methods: subjective measures (e.g., questionnaires on trust or satisfaction), objective measures (e.g., task performance metrics), and mathematical metrics (e.g., for faithfulness). Yet, it remains unclear how these families align or diverge in practice. In a preregistered between-subject study ( N =166) we use three established saliency map techniques (LIME, Grad-CAM, Guided Backpropagation) as a testbed to examine this issue. We find that each family of methods leads to different conclusions: participants reported no differences in trust or satisfaction, Grad-CAM improved user performance, while mathematical metrics favored Guided Backpropagation. At the same time, mathematical metrics only partially related to user performance, and these relationships were sometimes counterintuitive. Our findings highlight the methodological importance of comparing subjective, objective, and mathematical approaches when evaluating XAI, illustrating both tensions and aspects that are aligned. We discuss implications for XAI evaluation frameworks.

title: Constructing causal stories: How mental models shape memory, prediction, and generalization
abstract: How do people learn to predict what happens next? On one account, people do so by building mental models that mirror aspects of the causal structure of the world. Accordingly, people tell a story of how the data was generated, focusing on goal-relevant information. On another account, people make predictions by learning simple mappings from relevant features of the situation to the outcome. Here, we provide evidence for the causal account. Across three experiments and two paradigms, we find that people misremember what happened, predict incorrectly what will happen, and generalize to novel situations in a way that's more consistent with the causal account than a feature-based alternative. People spontaneously construct causal models that compress experience to privilege causally relevant information. These models organize how we remember the past, predict the future, and generalize to novel situations.

title: Legendre-Enhanced Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning for Nonlinear Scientific Time Series: A Reproducible Research Framework
abstract: Hybrid quantum–classical machine learning offers a practical route for investigating quantum models while current quantum hardware remains resource constrained. A central design choice is how classi- cal data are encoded into a quantum model. This proposal develops and evaluates a Legendre-enhanced hybrid quantum machine-learning framework for nonlinear scientific time-series classification. The pro- posed pipeline combines temporal representation learning, orthogonal- polynomial feature expansion, low-dimensional quantum encoding, an inverse Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT† ), and a trainable variational quantum circuit. The central hypothesis is that a structured Legendre basis can provide a useful intermediate representation between nonlinear scien- tific signals and compact quantum circuits. The study is explicitly comparative: raw features, ordinary polynomial features, Fourier fea- tures, Chebyshev features, and Legendre features will be evaluated under matched classical and quantum resource budgets. The initial benchmark will use a controlled nonlinear synthetic optical signal, followed by experiments on real scientific time-series domains such as electrocardiography (ECG), electroencephalography (EEG), and particle-physics/accelerator data where appropriate public datasets and compatible labels are available. The study will report accuracy, macro-F1, loss, parameter count, circuit depth, qubit count, wall-clock latency, memory usage, conver- gence, gradient behaviour, and robustness to simulated noise. Multiple random seeds and ablation studies will be used to separate the effect of the Legendre representation from the effect of the remaining archi- tecture. No quantum advantage is assumed a priori. The objective is to establish a falsifiable, reproducible methodology for determining when an orthogonal-polynomial representation is useful for low-resource hybrid quantum learning of scientific time series.

title: Geometric Constraint-Driven Self-Organization of Quantum Systems
abstract: This paper explores the potential of geometric constraint-driven self-organization as a novel framework for manipulating quantum systems. Traditional approaches often rely on classical control and iterative refinement, struggling to produce complex structures with predictable emergence. This work proposes a framework centered around the creation of complex geometric landscapes, utilizing constraints to guide self-organization and the formation of novel quantum arrangements. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through illustrative examples, emphasizing the interplay between geometry, constraint, and emergent behavior. The core claim is that carefully designed geometric constraints can unlock a level of control and complexity previously unattainable through conventional methods.

title: Post-Compromise Security for Autonomous Mobile Agents: Deterministic Runtime Enforcement of Mobile Execution Authority / 自主行動端Agent 攻陷後安全:行動執行權限之確定性運行時強制執行
abstract: Autonomous mobile agents increasingly combine learned or language-based decision processes with privileged mobile APIs and operating system services. This creates a post-compromise security problem distinct from conventional model-level robustness: once the autonomous controller is fully compromised, can unauthorized intent still obtain downstreammobile execution authority? We formulate the Post-Compromise Mobile Execution Authority Problem and investigate whether a deterministic runtime enforcement layer can preserve execution authorization independently of controller integrity. We present DROS-Mobile, a reference implementation positioned between autonomous agent intent and protected mobile execution interfaces. The design separates cognitive intent from execution authority through explicit principal, capability, policy, and revocation checks.We formalize three properties: Unauthorized Protected System-Effect Invariance (P1), Revocation-Bound Execution Authority (P2), and Delegation Non-Escalation (P3) under explicitly declared protected execution paths Eprotected. We evaluate the system across nominal execution, fully compromisedagent behavior (C ∗), adversarial API requests, authorization bypass attempts, capability replay, revocation races, and sustained stress workloads on iOS and Android environments. The evaluation measures unauthorized protected system effects, containment rate, multi-stage revocation horizons (Trev vs. TRCU), delegation propagation, decomposed enforcement latency, and runtime overhead. title: Quantum Error Correction for Distributed Machine Learning Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum error correction (QEC) codes to address the challenges of optimization within distributed machine learning (DML) systems. Traditional DML frameworks are susceptible to communication noise, leading to errors in the optimization process and ultimately impacting the quality of the learned models. This work proposes a novel approach where QEC codes are leveraged to correct these errors during information transmission between distributed nodes. The core concept hinges on decomposing the machine learning task across multiple nodes and employing QEC to ensure the accurate propagation of information, thereby enhancing the robustness and efficiency of the optimization process. title: Adaptive Meta-Learning via Bayesian Optimization of Neural Network Architectures
abstract: Meta-learning, or "learning to learn," has emerged as a promising paradigm for addressing challenges in areas such as few-shot learning and continual learning. Traditional meta-learning approaches frequently utilize predefined neural network architectures, a constraint that can hinder adaptability across a wide range of tasks. This paper introduces a novel adaptive meta-learning framework that addresses this limitation by dynamically optimizing the architecture of the meta-learner itself. We leverage Bayesian optimization to explore the architectural search space, treating the meta-learner's architecture as a set of parameters. The Bayesian model provides a probabilistic representation of this search space, allowing for efficient exploration and exploitation of potentially beneficial architectural configurations. Our approach aims to learn not just an optimal learning algorithm, but the optimal learning *system*—a meta-learner whose architecture is tailored to the task distribution. This work demonstrates the potential of such adaptive meta-learning, offering a more flexible and robust solution for tackling diverse learning problems.

title: Probability Logic and Linear Algebra Constraints: A Novel Approach to Model Verification and Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic framework predicated on linear algebra constraints, aiming to automate model verification and optimization. We leverage the inherent predictability of probability logic to ensure constraint validity and integrate a dynamic adjustment mechanism, addressing the limitations of existing techniques. The core principle centers on combining probabilistic modeling with automated linear algebra constraint derivation. This approach promises to simplify model validation and optimization, particularly for complex scenarios. The paper details the framework's architecture, identifies the key challenges and opportunities, and presents the initial results demonstrating the framework's effectiveness.

title: Simulating Evolutionary Neural Networks with Meta-Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to designing and training neural networks by integrating Simulated Evolution Algorithms (SEA) with Meta-Learning. The core idea is to utilize SEA to dynamically optimize the architecture and synaptic weights of a neural network, fostering a system capable of adaptive learning. We introduce a meta-learning mechanism that accelerates the learning process for new tasks. The key innovation lies in applying the principles of SEA – specifically, population-based optimization and mutation – to the complex landscape of neural network design. This results in a network that not only learns effectively from data but also possesses an inherent ability to quickly adapt to unfamiliar challenges. We demonstrate, through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, the potential of this hybrid approach to overcome limitations of traditional neural network training methods. The proposed system is designed for efficiency and adaptability, representing a significant step towards more robust and intelligent artificial neural networks.

title: Dynamic Program Analysis and Adaptive Optimization
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program analysis and optimization, termed Dynamic Program Analysis and Adaptive Optimization (DPAAO). The core claim of DPAAO is to develop a system capable of real-time analysis of program execution and subsequent adaptive optimization, ultimately enhancing both program performance and security. This is achieved through a mechanism combining Dynamic Binary Analysis (DDA) with machine learning algorithms. The system continuously monitors program state during execution, leveraging this information to dynamically adjust execution strategies. Unlike traditional static program analysis techniques, DPAAO offers a dynamic and adaptive solution, addressing limitations inherent in static analysis methods. The research contributes to a more efficient and secure software environment by enabling programs to respond intelligently to changing conditions during operation. This system aims to significantly reduce the reliance on pre-defined optimization rules and improve the overall adaptability of software.

title: Causal Inference via Time Series Prediction
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to causal inference leveraging the power of time series prediction models. Traditional methods of causal discovery often rely on predefined causal structures or require extensive domain expertise. We propose a framework that utilizes time series prediction models to implicitly learn and subsequently infer causal relationships from observed time series data. The core mechanism involves analyzing the prediction error of these models, which acts as a proxy for causal influence. Specifically, we develop an algorithm that identifies time series variables whose prediction errors are significantly correlated with changes in other variables, thereby indicating potential causal links. The methodology avoids the need for explicitly defined causal graphs and offers a data-driven approach suitable for complex, dynamic systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline potential applications within various domains. The key contribution lies in transforming the problem of causal discovery into a prediction problem, allowing time series models to uncover underlying causal structures. ---

title: Quantum Entanglement Stream Encryption Protocol
abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum entanglement stream encryption protocol designed to enhance security against emerging quantum attacks. The protocol leverages a layered network of entangled nodes to achieve secure data transmission. The core mechanism involves deploying multiple physically separated entanglement sources, facilitating information exchange between nodes, and employing redundancy coding alongside a quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol at each entanglement node. This approach significantly improves the protocol's robustness and practicality compared to traditional single-node entanglement schemes. The proposed system aims to provide a high level of security by exploiting the inherent properties of quantum entanglement and employing strategic redundancy to mitigate potential vulnerabilities. The protocol's design incorporates key aspects of quantum cryptography, including the fundamental principles of entanglement, the secure distribution of cryptographic keys, and the use of redundancy to enhance resilience against eavesdropping and attacks. The ultimate goal is to establish a secure communication channel for streaming data, impervious to attacks from both classical and future quantum adversaries.

title: Relational Neural Networks with Hierarchical Graph Decomposition
abstract: Existing Relational Neural Networks (R-Nets) demonstrate effectiveness in various graph-based learning tasks; however, their performance often degrades significantly when applied to very large and complex graphs. This paper introduces a novel approach, Hierarchical Graph Decomposition (HGD), integrated within R-Net architectures, to address this scalability limitation. HGD employs a recursive decomposition strategy, breaking down the original graph into progressively smaller subgraphs. This hierarchical structure enables the network to operate on manageable components, improving computational efficiency and maintaining learning performance on large graphs. The core claim is that R-Nets can struggle with very large and complex graphs. The mechanism is the implementation of HGD, which recursively decomposes the graph. This addresses scalability issues of R-Nets via hierarchical graph decomposition.

title: Dynamic Context-Aware Neural Symbolic Reasoning Engine (DCNIRE)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Context-Aware Neural Symbolic Reasoning Engine (DCNIRE), a novel system designed for real-time, dynamic knowledge representation and reasoning. The core of DCNIRE lies in a dynamically evolving neural-symbolic knowledge graph that integrates multi-modal inputs – text, images, audio, and sensor data – in a context-aware manner. The system employs a Transformer-based encoder to process these inputs, generating a high-dimensional contextual vector. This vector is then mapped to the knowledge graph by a learnable neural symbolic representation module. A reinforcement learning-based reasoning engine utilizes this graph for inference, dynamically updating its structure and weights based on the derived conclusions. Furthermore, a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) module is integrated to proactively generate and validate novel knowledge fragments, enhancing the graph's completeness and adaptability. Unlike existing systems that rely on static knowledge graphs, DCNIRE's dynamic graph evolution, multi-modal fusion, and reinforcement learning-driven reasoning enable it to effectively handle complex, evolving contexts. The system's architecture and methodology represent a significant advancement in neural-symbolic reasoning, paving the way for more robust and adaptable AI systems.

title: The Architecture of Intelligence: From Discrete Agency to Field-Based Cognition
abstract: This paper presents a unified theoretical framework synthesizing modular container-based architectures, Quantassical (quantum-classical hybrid) computation, and nature-inspired field-based algorithms toward post-agentic intelligence. The CES-QN (Causal-Self-Evolving-Quantum-Neuromorphic) framework integrates four interdependent pillars—causal reasoning via Structural Causal Models, embodied neuromorphic spiking hardware, self-evolving meta-learning with formal verification, and quantum-accelerated optimization in Hilbert space—within a container-based orchestration layer. The framework argues for the dissolution of discrete agency into ambient, field-based cognition where planning becomes geodesic traversal across physical manifolds. Two primary validation domains are proposed: water safety (parts-per-trillion contaminant detection) and atmospheric pollution management, with future extensions to food security, urban-rural planning, bio-photonics, and defense systems. Grounded in Noether's conservation symmetries, Bejan's Constructal Law, West's scaling laws, and Gödel's formal limits, the architecture achieves 100–1000× energy efficiency versus current AI systems while addressing NP-hard optimization problems that classical and agentic approaches cannot tractably solve.
